text: Every chapter in this course is a working part of the same SOC, and this capstone is where they stop being seven separate topics and start being the thing Lessons 29 through 31 just put into practice. People and process decide what an alert means, the platform gets the right data in front of them, detection logic turns raw events into alerts worth looking at, and automation and reporting keep the whole operation measurable instead of one analyst drowning in a queue.

Chapter 1 covered the SOC's mission, its tiered roles, and its shift models, which Lesson 29's Friday overnight shift put directly into practice. Chapters 2 and 3 covered what a SIEM actually does and how logs get collected and normalized into it, the pipeline behind every login record in this chapter. Chapter 4 covered correlation rules - exactly what Lesson 30 built from scratch and Lesson 31 watched fire for real against a genuine incident.

Chapter 5 covered the validate, scope, and classify triage process Jordan ran against all three of Lesson 29's alerts, reaching three different verdicts from the same steps. Chapter 6 covered dashboards, MTTD, and MTTR - what Lesson 31's closed case quietly became once it was resolved and reported upward. Chapter 7 covered SOAR, the exact kind of playbook that cut that case's response time from 40 minutes to under 3.

Lesson 31's case is the clearest proof this has to work as one system. A SIEM with no collection pipeline has nothing to correlate. A correlation rule with no triage process behind it just adds another unread alert to the queue. A confirmed incident with no SOAR playbook takes 40 minutes every time instead of 3, and none of it reaches leadership without a dashboard turning a closed case into a metric.

That's the full course: from one failed-login alert to a SOC that collects its own logs, correlates real detections, triages under pressure, automates its response, and reports its results upward. Course complete. Next up in this path: Microsoft Sentinel, Defender XDR, and KQL.
